Volume detail Last session (2026-11-16): 1.05× the 50-day average — about typical participation Lean: closed down 1.0%, mid-range, OBV falling — leans toward selling pressure Effort vs. result: 1.05× volume for 0.43× its own ATR of price progress — quiet on both counts — nothing to read here either way (thresholds are first-principles, not backtested) Last 20 days: bearish divergence — distribution warning Direction comes from daily bars (day change, where it closed in the day's range, OBV). Daily bars can't show actual buy or sell orders, so this is a lean, not a verdict. The effort-vs-result thresholds are first-principles, not backtested. What these numbers are The three tiles are common rules of thumb: at least 7 of 8 trend checks pass, RSI is between 50 and 70 (rising but not overheated), and the stock has done better than the S&P 500 over the past year. STA has not tested them, and they do not predict what happens next. They describe the stock; the decision is yours. Why only 4 checks are listed: the full score uses 8 checks from Mark Minervini's Trend Template. The 4 listed are the ones most traders lean on; the other 4 mostly repeat them. Trend strength (ADX): ADX measures how hard the price is pushing in one direction. Below 20 means it's moving sideways right now. In an uptrend that usually means resting, not a broken trend. Prices are adjusted for dividends: older prices (and so highs and averages) are lowered for dividends paid, so for a dividend payer they can sit a little below what the chart showed on the day. The 1-year high here and on the Price Data card are the same number. Slow vs fast averages: the trend checks use simple averages, which don't flip on a few noisy days. The price gauge uses a fast (exponential) 21-day average. Stops use neither; they're based on ATR. The price gauge and ladder show where the price sits against its 21, 50 and 200-day averages: the gauge in day-moves, the ladder in real dollars. It follows an old trading idea: buying far above the 21-day average means a farther stop (Livermore's pivotal points, O'Neil's "don't buy extended"). It shows for every stock and only measures; when to buy is your call.
